items.title: User flows
items.description: A user flow is a map of the steps someone takes to get something done. Draw it before you draw any screens.

metadata.youllNeed: Paper or a free Figma or FigJam file.
metadata.seoTitle: User flows for beginners: map the steps before you design screens
metadata.seoDescription: A user flow is a map of the steps someone takes to get something done. Learn the basic shapes, how to draw one, and why error paths matter.

quiz.question: What is the "happy path"?
options: The flow where everything goes right
quiz.why: It's the ideal route. The rest of the work is dealing with what happens when things don't go right.

quiz.question: Which shape is commonly used for a decision?
quiz.why: Flowcharts use diamonds for questions with different outcomes.

quiz.question: Why do error paths matter?
options: Many real problems happen when something fails, and people still need a way forward
quiz.why: A flow that only works when everything goes right will fail real people.

quiz.question: What should you pick before drawing a flow?
quiz.why: One goal keeps the flow clear and small.

items.title: Information architecture
items.description: Information architecture is how you organize and name things so people can find them without thinking.

metadata.seoTitle: Information architecture: organize things so people find them
metadata.seoDescription: Information architecture is how you group, name and structure content so people find it without thinking. Learn card sorting and sitemaps.

quiz.question: What is information architecture?
options: How content is organized, named and connected so people can find it
quiz.why: It's the structure that helps people find what they need.

quiz.question: In an "open" card sort, who creates the group names?
quiz.why: Open sorts show how people naturally group things. In closed sorts, you supply the names.

quiz.question: Whose words should you use for labels?
quiz.why: Labels work when people recognize them.

quiz.question: People can't find a feature. What's the likely IA problem?
options: It's grouped or labeled in a way that doesn't match how people think
quiz.why: Findability depends on structure and labels.

items.title: Sketching ideas fast
items.description: Your first idea is rarely your best. Sketch lots of rough ideas quickly, then pick the best one.

metadata.youllNeed: Paper, a pen and a timer.
metadata.seoTitle: Sketching ideas fast: why eight bad ideas beat one precious one
metadata.seoDescription: Your first idea is rarely your best. Learn a fast sketching drill, why paper beats Figma at this stage, and how to choose without ego.

quiz.question: Why sketch many ideas instead of one?
options: The first idea is rarely the best, and the better ones come later
quiz.why: Quantity helps you get past the obvious.

quiz.question: Why use paper at this stage?
options: It's fast and cheap, so you're not attached to what you draw
quiz.why: Low cost means you can throw ideas away freely.

quiz.question: What should you compare your sketches against?
options: Which best helps your user with the problem
quiz.why: The goal is solving the problem, not drawing.

quiz.question: You can't draw well. Should you skip sketching?
options: No, boxes and stick figures are fine
Ask someone else to do it
quiz.why: A sketch only has to show the idea.

items.title: Low-fi wireframes
items.description: A low-fi wireframe is a plain, grey-box blueprint of a screen. It's for deciding what goes where, not how it looks.

metadata.seoTitle: Low-fi wireframes: the floor plan of your screen
metadata.seoDescription: A low-fi wireframe is a plain, grey-box blueprint of a screen. Learn what to include, what to leave out, and how to build one in Figma.

quiz.question: What is a low-fi wireframe for?
options: Deciding what goes where before styling
quiz.why: It keeps attention on structure and hierarchy.

quiz.question: Which belongs in a low-fi wireframe?
quiz.why: Structure and words matter. Style comes later.

quiz.question: Why use real labels instead of lorem ipsum?
options: Placeholder text can hide problems with wording and space
quiz.why: Real words show if a button label is too long or unclear.

quiz.question: Which states should you include besides the perfect-data screen?
quiz.why: People will see these states, so they need to be planned.

items.title: Mobile vs desktop patterns
items.description: People hold phones with thumbs and use desktops with mice and keyboards. Good patterns respect that.

metadata.youllNeed: A free Figma account; your phone.
metadata.seoTitle: Mobile vs desktop design patterns: thumbs, mice and screens
metadata.seoDescription: People hold phones with thumbs and use desktops with mice and keyboards. Learn the common patterns for each and how to design for both.

quiz.question: Why do many phone apps put navigation at the bottom?
options: Thumbs reach the bottom easily when holding a phone
quiz.why: The bottom of the screen is easiest for a thumb to reach.

quiz.question: What should you avoid with hover?
quiz.why: Phones can't hover, and some people don't use a mouse.

quiz.question: Where can you find free, official guidance on platform patterns?
options: Apple's Human Interface Guidelines and Google's Material Design
quiz.why: Both are published and kept up to date by the platform makers.

quiz.question: On a wider screen, what should you do with a phone layout?
options: Rearrange it to use the space well
quiz.why: Stretching leaves awkward gaps and very long lines.

items.title: Testing early
items.description: Test your rough wireframes with a few real people before you build anything. Watching a handful of people struggle teaches more than guessing for weeks.

metadata.youllNeed: A friend or two; a clickable Figma prototype or paper screens.
metadata.seoTitle: Testing early: how to usability test a rough wireframe
metadata.seoDescription: Test rough wireframes with a few real people before you build anything. Learn how to run a simple usability test and turn findings into fixes.

quiz.question: When should you start testing?
quiz.why: Fixing a rough sketch is far cheaper than fixing built code.

quiz.question: A person gets stuck during a test. What do you do?
options: Stay quiet and note where they got stuck
quiz.why: Where people get stuck is exactly what you're there to learn.

quiz.question: What can a small test with about five people show you?
options: The biggest problems, not necessarily all of them
quiz.why: A small group is good at spotting major issues, but it doesn't prove everything.

quiz.question: How should you prioritize issues?
options: By how many people hit it and how much it blocks the goal
By how easy it is to fix
quiz.why: Fix what blocks people most first.
